newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Commodity markets unshaken by Deng's death.
newsitem.headline: Commodity markets unshaken by Deng's death.

text.p: China is a giant in world commodities and prices of raw materials from wheat to copper jump when this behemoth is buying, but barely a ripple stirred the markets on Thursday after the passing of Deng Xiaoping.

"He has been ill for a long time, and his death was not totally unexpected," a commodity trader in Singapore said. "I don't expect his passing to have any impact on China's buying programme, because players there are now more professional and market orientated."

But the fear of internal power struggles following the death of Deng, has injected a jarring note of uncertainty into markets which are acutely sensitive to Chinese moves due to the sheer scale of the trade flows they can generate.

The rising living standards of 1.2 billion people and their increasing demand for meat, dairy products and higher quality foods have stretched China's ability to feed itself and seen it emerge as the world's largest grain buyer.
Based on recent growth trends, some analysts predict China will account for nearly 20 percent of total international grain trade within the next decade.

"The China numbers in the past few years have been frightening," U.S. Feed Grains council analyst Erick Erickson said recently, referring to the abrupt switch from large exports to hefty imports. "The turnaround is so big," he said.
But the grain market was largely unmoved by Deng's death.

"As long as the current policies keep inflation down and the farmers are making money and the city people are eating -- hey, nobody would change that policy," a Western agriculture trade official in Shanghai told Reuters.

Grain traders, industry executives and diplomats throughout the Asia-Pacific region described China's current agriculture policies as a legacy of reforms Deng introduced in 1979 and accelerated in the past five years.
"He was the man that got it going," said a grain trader in Singapore, referring to Deng's policy of freeing farmers from the yoke of collective farming and state-set prices.
"I think there will a continuation of the policies put into place when he first started his reforms and that have been maintained and expanded on for the past four or five years."
Dealers in industrial commodities such as base metals and rubber were wary, but not unduely concerned by Deng's demise.

They said, however, that the reforms he set in place during an 18-year reign helped transform China into a major power in the marketplace, and any economic policy changes by Deng's successors that stunted the country's spectacular economic growth would dampen metals demand worldwide.
"If they turn to to a tighter-money policy, domestic demand for copper and zinc will decline," said one veteran Japaese industry analyst.

Although he saw little reason to expect such a policy shift any time soon, any sizeable drop in demand in China, the world's largest importer of refined copper and exporter of refined zinc, would reverberate throughout international markets.

China's influence on world metal markets was apparent just hours before Deng's death on Wednesday, when rumours that China was replenishing its strategic reserves helped propel prices on the London Metal Exchange to their highest levels in more than eight months.

Several analysts have raised their copper price forecasts in recent weeks, due in large part to expectations that strong demand from China will help absorb a surge in global mine production over the next several years.
China's copper imports rose nearly one-third last year to more than 700,000 tonnes.

It's hardly a surprise," the chief rubber trader at a commodity company in Singapore said of Deng's death. "He's been dead politically for five years. If there is a smooth transfer of power, it shouldn't have any impact," he said.
"There is potential for a short-term bearish impact (on the rubber market) if there is a power struggle in China, but the probability must be rather low."
